svg.title: claudia creates — rotating objects on a slide
svg.desc: A slide with a rotated picture, a rotated stamp and an arrow being turned with the handle; a text box held by another person; an object near the slide's edge; the history entries; open points.
svg.text: claudia creates — turning an object on the slide

For review before any code. Content is invented. Shared parts (handle, Format ▸ Rotate, Rotate By…) are mock-up 1; this is how they sit on a slide, next to the existing hold (D82), grid (D214) and history.
A · Turning an arrow on a slide
A picture and a stamp are already turned; you are dragging the arrow. Held objects show handles to you and your colour to others (D82).
Arrow 2 · a shape · held by you
A drag that is not finished is not
in the history: one entry on release.
Anna holds the stamp. You see her colour on its turned outline and her name on a tag
that stays upright. No handle for you; clicking it says why (D82).
Text box 3 is held by anna.
C · Turning near the slide's edge
The rule today keeps an object on the slide (geometry.ts). Proposed: the turned outline
is what must stay on, so a turn that would push a corner off nudges the object inward,
One undo puts back the turn and the nudge together.
The handle and its chip, as in mock-up 1. The chip shows 340°, not −20°: the model keeps 0–359.
A stamp turned to 348°: the text turns with the box, and so does the editor when you double-click to edit the words.
A picture turned 4°, the way a photo lies on a table; it keeps its proportions and its description.
The arrow's frame and handles turn with it. Resizing works along the object's own axes; the corner opposite the one you drag stays where it is on
History: “Rotate object” names the object by its own name (generated, renameable: Text box 3, Arrow 2). A turn by key, menu, popover or handle is one
Anna's outline turns with the object; only her name stays upright, at the corner of the object's turned bounding box.
The refusal is the one the hold already gives; nothing new to learn.
The pink strip is where the object would hang over the slide's edge.
Open points, with a recommendation each
1 Must the turned outline stay on the slide?
Recommended: yes, nudge in the same step. Otherwise: allow overhang, as most tools do,
and clip in the show and print.
2 Grid and snap on a turned object (D214)
Recommended: moving snaps the turned outline's edges; resizing a tilted edge is free,
since no grid line runs along it.
Not in this round: there are no groups yet (E10.6). Each object turns about its own
A slot's object turned by hand counts as “differs from its layout” (the dot on the tab,
